blocks.text: The *misafir*, the guest, has a special place in Turkish life. People visit each other often: for a holiday, a new baby or a new home, when someone is ill or has died, or just for tea. Hosts take pride in looking after their guests, and a visit follows a few customs that most families still keep. Even an unexpected visitor is welcome: Turkish calls one a *Tanrı misafiri*, a **guest of God**.
Guests rarely come empty-handed. A box of sweets or chocolates, some flowers, or something for the children is usual, and hosts generally don't open a present in front of the giver.

At the door, guests take off their shoes and leave them in the entrance, and the host often offers a pair of *terlik*, slippers; many homes keep a few pairs just for visitors. The first words are fixed. The host says *Hoş geldiniz* (welcome), the guest answers *Hoş bulduk* (as in [A1 unit 1](a1-u01)), and the host waves the guest in with *Buyurun*. Thanks for the visit come early too: *Ayağınıza sağlık*, literally **health to your feet**, a way of saying **how kind of you to come**.

Soon a bottle of *kolonya* comes round: a light cologne with a high alcohol content, between 60 and 80 per cent, which guests pour into their palms, rub into their hands and often pat on their face. Lemon is the classic scent; others are made with tobacco, lavender or flowers. Cologne reached the Ottoman Empire from Europe in the 19th century, and the first local brand dates from 1882. Since then it has been part of holiday visits and condolence visits alike, and when the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020, demand for it rose sharply: it is, after all, a ready-made hand sanitizer.

Then come tea or Turkish coffee, and usually something to eat: biscuits, fruit, a cake or a *börek* made that morning. Hosts offer again and again, and a first refusal is often taken for politeness, so a guest who really has had enough says so clearly, with a hand on the chest. A guest who has eaten thanks the cook with *Elinize sağlık*, **health to your hands**, one of the set wishes of the [next unit](gp-set-wishes). When the guests leave, the host sees them to the door with *Yine bekleriz*: **we'll expect you again**.
A proverb reminds guests of their side of the bargain:

blocks.en: A guest eats not what he hoped for, but what he finds.
blocks.source: Turkish proverb, as listed in the TDK dictionary

blocks.text: Here is a visit in the Turkish of this unit:

blocks.tr: Türk arkadaşınız sizi evine davet etti. Kapıda ayakkabılarınızı çıkarmalısınız, ama merak etmeyin: arkadaşınız size terlik verir. Sonra kolonya gelir: ellerinize biraz kolonya dökmelisiniz. Çay ve tatlı da hemen gelir. Her şeyi yemek zorunda değilsiniz, ama biraz yemeniz lazım!
blocks.en: A Turkish friend has invited you to their home. At the door you should take off your shoes, but don't worry: your friend will give you slippers. Then the cologne comes round: you should pour a little into your hands. Tea and something sweet soon follow. You don't have to eat everything, but you do need to eat a little!

vocab.en: to offer (food or drink to a guest)
Glad to be here (the reply to welcome).
Thank you for the food (to the cook).
Come again. We'll expect you again.

questions.q: What does a guest usually do at the door?
options: takes off his or her shoes

questions.q: When does a guest say *Elinize sağlık*?
options: after eating food the host has made
questions.explain: **Health to your hands**: the hands that cooked the meal.

questions.q: In the Turkish text, what don't you have to do?
questions.explain: *Her şeyi yemek zorunda değilsiniz*: you don't have to eat everything.

sources.title: Turkish Culture: Etiquette
sources.note: Shoes taken off at the door, slippers offered; sweets, flowers or presents for the children, usually not opened in front of the giver; tea or coffee offered at once; food offered repeatedly, a first refusal, a hand on the chest to decline firmly; Elinize sağlık to compliment the cook

sources.title: Kolonya
sources.note: Cologne first imported from Germany in the 19th century; 60 to 80 per cent ethyl alcohol; often offered to guests in Turkish homes; used as a hand sanitizer

sources.title: Kolonya
sources.note: Reached the Ottoman Empire in the late 19th century; first local production in 1882 (Faruki Colonia); lemon the most widely preferred scent; offered to guests on holiday and condolence visits; demand and production rose during the COVID-19 pandemic

sources.title: kolonya, misafir, ayağına sağlık
sources.note: kolonya: a light alcoholic liquid scented with lemon, lavender, tobacco and other plants; ayağına sağlık: said to mean that someone's coming has pleased you; under misafir, Tanrı misafiri and the proverb “misafir umduğunu değil bulduğunu yer”
